opus-5.5.text:
So the way I think about wake-sleep, at least the way we used it in DreamCoder, is that it's really about the interplay between two kinds of learning that a system needs if it's going to get better at solving problems over time.

During the "wake" phase, the system is out in the world, so to speak. It's given real problems, in our case programming tasks or things like drawing pictures or building towers, and it tries to solve them by searching for programs. That search is expensive and hard, but when it succeeds you get real experience: here's a problem, here's a program that solves it.

Then there's the "sleep" phase, which in our version has two parts. One is what we called abstraction, sort of consolidating that experience. You look back over the programs you've found and ask, what patterns keep recurring? Can I pull those out as new reusable concepts, new library functions, so that the next time I face a similar problem the solution is shorter and easier to find? That grows a domain-specific language, and the knowledge is explicit and symbolic, so you can inspect it.

The other part of sleep is dreaming. The system samples programs from its current library, runs them to see what they produce, and uses those imagined problem-solution pairs to train a neural network that guides search. So you're training intuition on fantasies, essentially, plus replays of real experience. That matters because you'll never have enough real data to train a good recognition model, but you can generate as much as you want from your own generative model.

The philosophy underneath is that expertise has these two complementary components. One is declarative knowledge: the concepts and vocabulary an expert has, which in our case is the library. The other is procedural, intuitive knowledge: knowing where to look and which ideas are likely relevant, which is the neural search policy. Wake-sleep is a way of bootstrapping both together. A better library makes the dreams richer and more relevant, and better intuitions let you solve harder problems while awake, which gives you more material to abstract from. It's a virtuous cycle.

There's a lineage here, of course. Hinton and colleagues had the original wake-sleep algorithm in the Helmholtz machine, where the idea was to train a recognition model and a generative model against each other. We took that spirit and applied it to program synthesis, where the generative model is a library of code and the recognition model guides the search. I find it a compelling picture of how a learner could grow, not just fitting a fixed hypothesis space but expanding the language it thinks in, and getting more fluent in that language as it goes.

r001.rationale: It describes sampling programs, running them to generate imagined problem-solution pairs, and training the neural search guide on those pairs, conveying an inverse search process learned from forward-generated examples.

r002.rationale: It mentions drawing pictures as a task domain, but does not compare rendering an image from 3D structure with inferring 3D structure from an image.

r003.rationale: It says wake-phase solutions are abstracted into the library, then sleep-phase dreams are sampled from the current library, so wake experience changes later synthetic examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The way I think about wake-sleep is that it's fundamentally about the relationship between a generative model and a recognition model, and about how you can bootstrap both of them off each other even when you don't have the kind of supervision you'd ideally want.

So the original Hinton wake-sleep algorithm from the nineties was about training a Helmholtz machine. You have a generative model that goes from latents to observations, and a recognition model that goes the other way, from observations to latents. And the problem is that inference in the generative model is hard. If you had a good inference procedure you could just do EM or something like it, but you don't. So the trick is: during the wake phase, you take real data, you use your recognition model to guess the latents, and you train the generative model to explain that data given those latents. During the sleep phase, you flip it. You dream up samples from the generative model, where now you actually know the latents because you generated them, and you train the recognition model on those fantasies. You get free supervision for the hard direction by sampling from the easy direction.

What I find philosophically interesting about that is the idea that a system can manufacture its own training data for the part of itself that's hardest to train. That's a very different stance from the standard supervised learning picture. It's self-supervision in a very literal sense: the model is its own teacher, and the two halves are each other's curriculum.

When we built DreamCoder, we took that structure and pushed it into program synthesis, which is a setting where it fits almost unreasonably well. The generative model there isn't a neural net, it's a library of code, a DSL plus a prior over programs built from that library. The recognition model is a neural network that looks at a task and proposes which pieces of the library are likely to be relevant. And the latents are programs. So the wake phase is: here are real problems, search for programs that solve them, guided by the neural net. And the sleep phase splits into two things. One is the classic sleep, where we sample random programs from the library, run them to get input-output examples, and train the recognition network on those dreams. The other is what we called abstraction sleep, where you look at the programs you found during waking and ask, what's the common structure here, what should I refactor out into a new library primitive?

That second piece is where I think the philosophy gets richer than the original algorithm. Because now the generative model isn't just getting better at explaining the same data, it's changing its representational vocabulary. The latent space itself is growing. And that changes what the recognition model can even express. So you get this loop where better concepts make search easier, easier search finds more solutions, more solutions give you material for new concepts. It's a kind of ratchet.

I also like that there's a plausible cognitive story. Nobody thinks the brain literally runs this algorithm, but the idea that you consolidate during offline periods, that you replay and compress experience, that you train fast heuristic processes on slower deliberate ones, those all have echoes in how people talk about memory consolidation and skill acquisition. You can be a bit skeptical of the biological analogies, but I think at the level of computational principle, there's something real there: a system with a slow, expensive, correct-ish process and a fast, cheap, approximate process, where the fast one is trained to imitate the slow one, and the slow one is accelerated by the fast one. That pattern shows up everywhere. It's AlphaZero, it's amortized inference, it's arguably what a lot of distillation is doing.

The limitation, and I'll be honest about it, is that dreams are only as good as your generative model. Early on, the random programs you sample are mostly garbage, and the recognition network is learning from garbage. So in practice you lean heavily on the wake phase, on replaying actual solved tasks, and the pure dreaming is more of a regularizer than the main signal. That's a departure from the original algorithm, and I think it reflects something true about learning in general: fantasy is useful, but it has to be anchored to reality often enough that it doesn't drift.

r001.rationale: It explains that the recognition model learns the inverse mapping from observations to latents using labeled dream samples generated by the generative model.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the ease of rendering an image from 3D structure with the difficulty of inferring 3D structure from an image.

r003.rationale: It says programs found during waking are used to add library primitives, changing the generative model's vocabulary; sleep then samples programs from that library to create training examples.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about wake-sleep learning is that you have two complementary problems. One is: given some observations, what latent explanation could have produced them? The other is: given an explanation, what observations would it produce?

In the wake phase, you start with actual data and try to infer the hidden structure behind it. In the sleep phase, you run your generative model forward—you imagine possible hidden structures and the data they would generate—and use those examples to train your inference mechanism. You know the explanation for those imagined examples because you generated them yourself.

So the philosophy is that learning from the world and learning from your own model of the world can reinforce each other. Inference helps you build a better model, and the model supplies practice that makes inference faster. For program learning, that means alternating between finding programs that explain tasks and generating synthetic tasks from programs, so you can learn to recognize which programs are likely to solve a new task.

r001.rationale: It says the sleep phase runs the generative model forward and uses the resulting imagined examples, whose explanations are known, to train the inference mechanism.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the ease of rendering an image from 3D structure with inferring 3D structure from an image.

r003.rationale: It describes wake and sleep learning as reinforcing each other, but does not say that wake-cycle problem-solving adjusts the synthetic-data distribution for subsequent sleep cycles.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the philosophy is that learning to understand the world and learning to generate it ought to support one another. You have a generative model that says, “Here’s how an observation could have come about,” and a recognition model that works in the other direction: “Given this observation, what latent explanation might have produced it?”

During wake, you take real observations, infer explanations, and use those explanations to improve the generative model. During sleep, you generate imagined observations from the model, where you know the latent causes, and train the recognition model to recover those causes.

So you’re using inference to help learn a model, and using the model to help learn inference. The appealing idea is that internally generated experience can provide its own training signal. The limitation is that your dreams reflect your current model: if that model is wrong, you can become very good at interpreting a world that doesn’t quite match reality.

r001.rationale: It describes generating observations from the model with known latent causes, then training the recognition model to recover those causes—the inverse process learned from synthetic examples.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the ease of rendering an image from 3D structure with inferring 3D structure from an image.

r003.rationale: It says wake inference on real observations improves the generative model, which then generates imagined observations during sleep, conveying that wake experience updates the source of later synthetic data.
